newsitem.title: UK: Mideast VLCCs steady ahead of Easter.
newsitem.headline: Mideast VLCCs steady ahead of Easter.

text.p: Middle East very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates were steady on Thursday after a rush of fixtures earlier in the week before the long Easter weekend, brokers said.

Galbraith's Ltd said in their weekly tanker report, "Volume of tonnage showing as available in the second half of April would suggest that unless there is a spectacular amount of fixing next week, rates may ease a little further."
Rates for modern VLCCs on Mideast/east voyages were around W62.5/65, and W52.5 to the U.S. Gulf.

Galbraith's noted that West Africa/U.S. Gulf rates have slipped to W70, "although though even at this level owners are making very much greater returns than they could achieve by ballasting back to the Arabian (Middle East) Gulf."

The Mediterranean market was quiet after the 80,000 tonne sector firmed to W145 earlier in the week. "Some owners feel that as there is a stoppage for Easter they may have to go for below W130 to get business," an Italian broker said.
Inter-U.K./Cont 80,000 tonners slipped to W135 from W140 but remain some 20 points above early March levels due to a dearth of quality tonnage for early dates, brokers said.
Fuel oil in UKC and the Med was steady and quiet, with 25,000 tonne cargoes at about W200 and W210 respectively.

Caribs/upcoast 70,000 tonners remained extremely firm at W240, more than 100 points above the February average of W131.6, according to New York-based Rigos Chartering Inc. Opinions were divided whether the spectacular strength in this traditionally volatile sector will last.
"For the owner, the outlook is still good with little tonnage available in the first half of April and almost non-existent prior to the 11th.

"Despite the impression that this is just another Caribbean blip, and that it will tumble as quickly as it rose, it has lasted longer than normal, and looks set to continue for the next few weeks," said Galbraith's.

But a New York broker disagreed. "It depends on the weather and what happens on the Mississippi where traffic has been slowed by a capsized barge, but I think rates will start to soften," he said. -- Michael Rank, London newsroom +44 171 542 4088
